before: A farming district uses all its land, labour and equipment to produce maize and cattle. Its yearly production schedule is A (0 t maize, 80 cattle), B (50 t, 75), C (100 t, 60), D (150 t, 35) and E (200 t, 0). Use the schedule to draw the district's production possibility curve (PPC), with maize on the horizontal axis. Plot J (50 t, 40 cattle) and K (100 t, 80 cattle) and state what each shows. Show the change from C to D and state its opportunity cost (4).
after: A farming district fully and efficiently uses its fixed land, labour and equipment to produce maize and cattle. Its yearly production schedule is A (0 t maize, 80 cattle), B (50 t, 75), C (100 t, 60), D (150 t, 35) and E (200 t, 0). Use the schedule to draw the district's production possibility curve (PPC), with maize on the horizontal axis. Plot J (50 t, 40 cattle) and K (100 t, 80 cattle) and state what each shows. Show the change from C to D and state its opportunity cost (4).

before: A shop sells 100 packets a week of maize meal and 100 packets a week of one brand of crisps, each at N$20 a packet. Both prices rise to N$30. Weekly sales of maize meal fall to 75 packets and sales of the crisps fall to 25 packets. Use these data to draw both demand curves on the same axes, with price on the vertical axis. Show the change for each product and label each curve with its price elasticity of demand (PED), calculated from the initial values (4).
after: A shop sells 100 packets a week of maize meal and 100 packets a week of one brand of crisps, each at N$20 a packet. Both prices rise to N$30. Weekly sales of maize meal fall to 75 packets and sales of the crisps fall to 25 packets. Assume straight demand lines and unchanged other demand conditions. Use these data to draw both demand curves on the same axes, with price on the vertical axis. Show the change for each product and label each curve with its price elasticity of demand (PED), calculated from the initial values (4).

before: Two furniture workshops each supply 50 chairs a month at N$400 a chair. The price rises to N$600. Workshop A, which has unused machines, increases supply to 90 chairs a month; workshop B, already at full capacity, increases supply to 60 chairs a month. Use these data to draw both supply curves on the same axes, with price on the vertical axis. Show the change for each workshop and label each curve with its price elasticity of supply (PES), calculated from the initial values (4).
after: Two furniture workshops each supply 50 chairs a month at N$400 a chair. The price rises to N$600. Workshop A, which has unused machines, increases supply to 90 chairs a month; workshop B, already near capacity, increases supply to 60 chairs a month. Assume straight supply lines and unchanged other supply conditions. Use these data to draw both supply curves on the same axes, with price on the vertical axis. Show the change for each workshop and label each curve with its price elasticity of supply (PES), calculated from the initial values (4).
